papers.title: How well does graph superoptimization transfer? Adapting tensor-graph superoptimizer to a Triton-based NPU
papers.abstract: For automatic optimization systems, performance portability across increasingly diverse AI accelerators remains a challenge. We investigate how well graph-level superoptimization transfers across architectures by adapting Mirage from its CUDA-oriented design to the Huawei Ascend 910B3 through a Triton-based compilation stack. We evaluate the adapted system on transformer-relevant workloads, including matrix multiplication, softmax, RMSNorm+MatMul, gated MLP, FNN, and attention. The results show that graph-level optimization can successfully transfer and outperform available reference implementations by up to 87.0% on fused workloads. However, performance is highly dependent on tensor shape and workload structure, with substantial regressions for other configurations. We identify target-specific tensor partitioning, execution-resource modeling, backend lowering and fusion, and search and verification costs as key limitations. Our findings demonstrate that a portable graph representation and programming model do not imply a portable optimization space, motivating modular target-specific mechanisms within otherwise reusable compiler infrastructure.

papers.title: DeltaHarness: Self-Evolving Harnesses for Resource-Adaptive Tool Execution
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents rely on execution harnesses to organize and schedule tool operations. The same task and resource description can conceal runtime conditions that reverse the latency ordering of valid execution plans. Resolving this uncertainty requires firsthand execution in the target setting. We introduce DeltaHarness, an execution-guided policy-search method that adapts agent harnesses from cold-start measurements. Its QHI loop uses the observed response to update runtime dispatch, revise physical plans, and select experiments for later proposals. An independent confirmation panel controls policy replacement. With fixed dispatch, a revised materialization policy reduces complete-delivery latency by 30.0% on one video-editing task across three fresh pairs. On held-out tasks, the evolved policies reduce latency by 8.2% relative to the best fixed plan in one seed and by 4.6% relative to the initial proposal in another.

papers.title: RyBench: Runtime Verification Benchmarking Framework over Publish/Subscribe Networks
papers.abstract: Autonomous systems built as distributed, node-based systems communicate via publish/subscribe middleware. Runtime Verification (RV) tools are used to monitor those systems against formal specifications, receiving monitored events through the pub/sub channel. An RV tool's practical value depends on its monitoring throughput capacity and verdict latency, besides its correctness, so a systematic benchmarking setup is needed to evaluate how efficiently these tools run. This paper presents RyBench, a pub/sub-based benchmarking framework that acts as a synthetic event publisher in place of a monitored system, providing a common benchmarking setup. RyBench separates benchmark generation, serialization, and transport into distinct components, enabling the combination of different event-generation strategies, data formats, and transport layers. We also evaluate the framework's throughput capacity across these configurations using Open Simulation Interface (OSI) schemas and Timescales properties, and illustrate the end-to-end benchmarking flow through an application to Reelay and an integration with MonPoly.

papers.title: On Traffic Characterization in Time-Sensitive Networking and Deterministic Networking
papers.abstract: The traffic of an audio/video stream in IEEE Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) or an asynchronous traffic flow in IETF Deterministic Networking is specified by three parameters: an observation time interval, a maximum packet size, and a maximum number of packets in the interval. This traffic specification (TSpec) triggers three fundamental questions for TSN and DetNet: (1) if and how the traffic of a flow can be specified by these parameters after it traverses a system, (2) how to specify the traffic of a flow aggregate using the three parameters, and (3) how to use it in performance guarantee analysis. Among them, the literature has focused on (3), leaving the other two little investigated and largely open. This paper is intended to bridge the gap. Specifically, we introduce an equivalent traffic characterization for TSN TSpec, which is simple in representation and simplifies analytical development. Based on this result, we establish an output characterization property for (1) and show that the output of a TSN flow traversing a bounded-delay system can be characterized by the TSN TSpec with updated parameters. For (2) we study the superposition of TSN flows and derive TSN traffic characterizations for the aggregate of multiple TSN flows. For (3), based on a relationship between the TSN traffic characterization and the well-known token-bucket traffic characterization, backlog and delay bounds are derived. Together, these results form a calculus for TSN traffic characterization.

papers.title: Critical heavy traffic and diffusion limits for shortest-of-d dynamic routing
papers.abstract: We study shortest-of-$d$ routing, with fixed $d\ge2$, in $N$ parallel queues with independent finite-state Markov service environments switching at rate $\kappa_N$. At the critical load $\rho_N=1-1/N$, the empirical measure of the centered queue lengths, under stationarity, converges in distribution to a random probability measure determined by its mean. We identify the mean's density and the conditional independence of fixed finite collections of centered queues in the limit. On time scales of order $N$, the centered empirical mean converges to a diffusion with explicit drift and constant diffusion coefficient. These limits hold when $\kappa_N/N\to\infty$, along subsequences with convergent lattice phase. The diffusion limit extends to centered initial empirical measures tight in the first Wasserstein topology, with means converging in law. A short initial layer prepares the limiting family while preserving the limiting mean. Empirical approximation holds in time-integrated Wasserstein distance.

papers.title: Why Kubernetes Cannot Contain a Full Lazy-Pulling Cache: Two Impossibility Results and a Bounded, Honest Design for Model Serving
papers.abstract: Lazy container-image pulling makes cold starts of autoscaled model-serving fleets on Kubernetes nearly independent of model size, but it moves the model's bytes into a node-level cache that the platform neither bounds nor accounts for. This article establishes, by experiment, two impossibility results for that cache. A monitoring-side remedy cannot catch its failure: a sentinel readiness probe stays green while 272 of 280 files are unreadable. A platform-side remedy cannot contain it: kubelet, given full disk-pressure visibility, frees 0 bytes by image garbage collection and falls back to evicting pods (26 across the campaign, the reading pod among them), because its reclamation actuator is keyed to an accounting that does not know the cache exists. The article then eliminates the failure class inside the component that owns the bytes, with no change to kubelet or the container runtime interface, by two design rules: a byte budget whose pressure signal is keyed to filesystem truth, so that a never-blocking, lossy accounting still enforces a hard bound (held against about 301,000 dropped updates), and pass-through semantics under which a failed cache write never becomes a failed read, with the coupling traced to a single io.MultiWriter. Across six pre-specified campaigns on AWS, upstream stargz-snapshotter fails 273 of 280 model files at 90% cache pre-fill; the proposed system reads all 150.3 GB with zero errors at +18.5% completion cost and holds the budget under a live read, co-tenancy, and a three-node fleet. A source audit shows the missing bound generalizes to SOCI and Nydus. The implementation is open source and has been proposed upstream.

papers.title: LEGIT: Live Eligibility Gating over Identifier Tries for Constrained Decoding of Heterogeneous Pages
papers.abstract: A generative recommender names each candidate with a short token sequence, a Semantic ID, and recommends by generating those tokens. Some generative recommenders, including the Uber Eats search engine we are building, write a whole results page, stores with their menu items, in one decoding pass. Every Semantic ID on such a page must name a real store or item that is eligible for the search, such as a store that delivers to the user's location, and that is not already on the page. Each item must also belong to the store above it. A trie over the catalog keeps identifiers real, but eligibility and repetition change with every request and token, and the grammar-constrained decoder we tried could not enforce these changing rules exactly and quickly. We call this constraint LEGIT, for live eligibility gating over identifier tries. Numbering trie leaves depth first turns each rule into a range lookup over one store trie and one item trie, and every generated page passes an independent catalog check. On one NVIDIA B200 GPU with one or two requests per decode step, a direct implementation that walks the trie on the GPU makes each token about 5 times as slow as unconstrained decoding. Across 36 implementations, hardware counters and ablations are consistent with kernel launches and CPU-GPU waits as the source of this slowdown. Our fastest implementation walks the trie on the CPU while the GPU runs the model, needs no custom kernel, and cuts time per output token by 65.9 percent against the direct GPU implementation, to about 1.7 times the unconstrained cost. This implementation is also the fastest on a page layout that puts each item before its store.

papers.title: Optimizing Winograd Convolution on ARMv8 processors
papers.abstract: As Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) gain increasing prominence in deep learning, algorithms such as Winograd convolution have been introduced to boost computational efficiency. However, existing Winograd implementations often face challenges, including significant transformation overhead, suboptimal computation efficiency, and reduced parallel performance in certain layers. In this work, we present an ARMv8-specific execution framework for Winograd convolution based on a cache-resident, block-wise schedule. By maintaining consecutive memory access where possible and packing data in a customized z-shaped layout, our approach fully exploits a meticulously optimized GEMM micro-kernel that employs a ping-pong technique. Furthermore, we introduce a multidimensional parallelization strategy that selects a thread decomposition across the batch, tile, input-channel, and output-channel loops according to layer shape and coordinates the resulting thread groups with the fused block-wise execution schedule. To further boost performance, we manually optimize each micro-kernel in AArch64 assembly, carefully tuning blocking parameters for the ARMv8 architecture to minimize transformation overhead and maximize computational throughput. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves up to $4.74\times$, $4.10\times$, $4.72\times$, and $10.57\times$ speedups over NCNN, NNPACK, FastConv, and ACL, respectively, on the Kunpeng 920 platform when using multiple threads, with corresponding gains of $5.46\times$, $2.81\times$, $6.11\times$, and $8.05\times$ on the AWS Graviton2, and $3.32\times$, $3.68\times$, $5.84\times$, and $9.28\times$ on the Phytium 2000+.

papers.title: Warpline: Binary-Level Tracing and Unified Evidence for Agentic GPU Kernel Optimization
papers.abstract: LLM agents are becoming GPU kernel engineers, but they still tune kernels without seeing where the time goes. Hardware profilers report how busy each unit was, not where each warp's time went; intra-kernel tracers can show it, but only with hand-placed probes and a recompilation that alters the very kernel being measured. We present Warpline, which gives agents this view automatically while leaving the kernel essentially unchanged. Warpline analyzes the binary to decide which events to record and inserts probes into the binary itself without recompilation or any manual step. It then aligns the trace with hardware profiling data on one unified timeline. Because it needs only the binary, it can regenerate this evidence for every new version of the kernel at whatever level the agent edits it (source, IR, or PTX), closing the optimization loop without human intervention. On NVIDIA B200, across 35 kernels in Triton, CuTe DSL, and CUDA C++, Warpline adds a median overhead of 1.2% and leaves a median 99.9% of executed instructions unchanged, whereas existing tracers have median overheads of 1.6% to 13.2% and leave only 4.6% to 32.7% unchanged. Warpline also traces closed-source kernels, which these tracers cannot. On 10 SOL-ExecBench problems, agents using Warpline spend less time and fewer model requests than a bare coding agent and NVIDIA's Kernel Design Agents (KDA), yet lead both after every round in geometric mean and reach a 7.69$\times$ geometric-mean speedup, against 6.94$\times$ and 6.13$\times$. Two case studies further demonstrate that Warpline reveals hidden bottlenecks and provides actionable optimization insights.
